citeAs: Krishna, R., Zhu, Y., Groth, O., Johnson, J., Hata, K., Kravitz, J., Chen, S., Kalantidis, Y., Li, L.-J., Shamma, D. A., Bernstein, M. S., Fei-Fei, L. (2016). Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations. International Journal of Computer Vision.
creator: Ranjay Krishna, Yuke Zhu, Oliver Groth, Justin Johnson, Kenji Hata, Joshua Kravitz, Stephanie Chen, Yannis Kalantidis, Li-Jia Li, David A. Shamma, Michael S. Bernstein, Li Fei-Fei
description: Visual Genome is a crowdsourced dataset for comprehensive scene understanding that contains densely annotated images with region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. The first release uses 108,249 images and grounds visual concepts to language, including canonicalization to WordNet synsets.
name: Visual Genome
rai:annotationsPerItem: Region descriptions: 50 per image; question-answer pairs: 8 freeform QAs plus around 20 region-based QAs per image tasking; verification uses 3 workers per annotation.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique Amazon Mechanical Turk workers contributed. 93.02% of workers were from the United States, 1.29% from the Philippines, 1.13% from Kenya, 0.94% from India, 0.50% from Russia, 0.47% from Canada, and 2.65% from other countries. The worker pool was 54.15% male and 45.85% female, with most workers aged 25 to 34; the youngest contributor was 18 and the oldest was 68.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All data were verified after annotation. All components except objects were verified by majority voting from three unique workers, and an annotation was added if at least two of the three workers judged it correct. Objects were verified using rapid judgments to speed verification. The paper also reports canonicalization evaluation scores: objects 88.0 precision / 98.5 recall, attributes 85.7 precision / 95.9 recall, and relationships 92.9 precision / 88.5 recall.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk through multiple task stages. Workers drew bounding boxes and wrote region descriptions, extracted objects and grounded them with boxes, added attributes and relationships to form region graphs, wrote freeform and region-based question-answer pairs, confirmed object co-reference for scene graph construction, and verified annotations using majority voting or rapid judgments. Workers were instructed to write diverse descriptions, use bounding boxes with coverage and quality, and write precise, unambiguous questions starting with one of the question words.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that the dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people. It also explicitly designed the collection process to reduce bias toward easy, frequently occurring relationships and common phrases by encouraging diverse region descriptions, showing workers similar prior descriptions, enforcing BLEU-based dissimilarity thresholds, and filtering against globally common descriptions like 'sky is blue'.
rai:dataCollection: Visual Genome was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. The first release uses 108,249 images from the intersection of YFCC100M and MS-COCO. The dataset was collected over 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration, with approximately 800,000 AMT HITs covering descriptions, questions and answers, and region graphs.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The first release uses 108,249 real-world, non-iconic images from the intersection of YFCC100M and MS-COCO. The images were uploaded onto Flickr by users and range from 72 pixels wide to 1280 pixels wide, with an average width of 500 pixels.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that the images are somewhat biased towards people. It also states that canonicalization mappings are not perfect and still contain some ambiguity. Some descriptions contain no explicit objects and therefore have no region graphs associated with them.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Post-collection processing included extracting objects, attributes, and relationships from region descriptions; merging co-referenced objects across region graphs into scene graphs using overlap heuristics with worker confirmation; and canonicalizing objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in descriptions and QAs to WordNet synsets.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset pipeline includes extraction of objects from descriptions, extraction of attributes and relationships, construction of region graphs and scene graphs, and canonicalization of objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in descriptions and QAs to WordNet synsets. The authors use Stanford dependency parsing and Stanford NLP tools as suggestions for noun phrase extraction, morphology-based normalization for attributes, sentence-frame-based mapping for relationships, and hand-crafted rules for common WordNet mapping failures.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training and benchmarking computer vision models for comprehensive scene understanding, including image description, dense image captioning, visual question answering, relationship extraction, semantic image retrieval, and structured scene graph reasoning.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford dependency parser and Stanford NLP tools were used to automatically extract nouns or noun phrases as suggestions for workers, and WordNet was used in the canonicalization pipeline.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotator demographics were collected, including country distribution, age distribution, and gender distribution of crowd workers.
